content.thinking:
I'm designing a gray wolf model in a Blizzard-style stance—chunky proportions, oversized paws, exaggerated head and shoulders—sketching out body dimensions and coordinate placement before building the full module.

Working out the skeleton: hips root joint, then a spine chain curving up to the chest, a neck chain branching off the spine tip, and a head joint positioned at the neck's end, with a jaw joint planned next off the head.

For the tail, I'm laying out a three-span catmull path hanging back and down from the hips into tail1, tail2, tail3 joints. Now I'm thinking about whether the body mesh should be a sweep along the combined tail-hips-spine path, or just skinned separately to those chains.

For the body, I'll sweep along the spine chain starting at hips, extending the rump backward slightly and defining an elliptical radius function that tapers from a narrower rump to a deep, barrel-like chest, matching a wolf's deep-chested build with roughly 0.9 length from hips to chest.

For Blizzard, I'll make the body slightly chunkier and broader than the wolf, widening the elliptical radii and possibly shifting the profile down to suggest a belly. For coloring, I'm defining a gray-toned palette (gray, dark, light, cream, brown) and planning to use mottled fur noise combined with countershading for a hand-painted look with a lighter belly.

Writing custom paint logic...

Still defining leg geometry...

Still shaping paw geometry...

Working out limb chains and naming with side suffixes based on x-coordinate sign, then setting up how the joint points get swept into tapered leg geometry with decreasing radii from shoulder to wrist.

Now I'm figuring out hind leg proportions digitigrade-style, calculating thigh, shin, and metatarsus segment lengths against the hip-to-foot distance, and working out bend directions at the knee and hock.

That seems too large for a folded leg, so I try shorter segment lengths instead, recalculating the vertical drop and solving the triangle to find how far forward the knee and hock should offset horizontally.

For the front legs, I'm computing the hip-to-foot distance and checking it against the segment lengths to see how straight or bent the elbow and wrist need to be, then setting up naming conventions for each leg chain so I can sweep tube geometry along them.

I'm adding haunch and shoulder muscle blobs as scaled spheres at the hip and shoulder joints to give the legs some bulk, and defining a paint function for the legs that blends tan and gray tones with a darker stripe running down the front based on surface normal and height.

For paws I'm picking a muted gray-brown tone with dark claws for contrast, considering a few color options before settling on a dark charcoal for readability. Now I'm moving on to building the oversized head shape manually using the head joint's local frame.

Working out skull and muzzle geometry...

For coloring, I'll apply countershading so the muzzle is gray-brown on top and fades to cream underneath, reusing the existing belly-cream logic based on vertical position. The nose gets a small dark flattened sphere at the muzzle tip, no gloss needed.

Now I'm building the lower jaw as a tapering sweep from the jaw joint forward to a tip point, using an elliptical cross-section function that narrows toward the front, then adding upper canine fangs as spikes projecting from the muzzle sides.

Adding lower canines and small incisor teeth...

I'm also deciding whether to pose the jaw slightly open by rotating it a few degrees about its hinge axis, planning to build all the jaw geometry first and apply that rotation afterward so the bone transform carries the attached parts with it.

Now I'm adding a dark interior mouth sweep and a small pink tongue tube, then moving on to shaping upright triangular wolf ears using an extruded outline with sharp points for an alert look.

Positioning the ears requires careful orientation vectors—I want them tilted slightly outward from the skull, but I'm wary that tilting the y-axis introduces a shear since x and y won't stay perfectly perpendicular. I'll accept a slight imperfection here rather than overcomplicate the transform.

For the ear design itself, I'm layering a gray outer shape with a smaller pink-cream inner ear piece positioned slightly forward and thin, plus a small fur tuft detail.

I'm working out the ear placement math -- figuring out the right world-space offset from the head's position so the ear sits mirrored correctly on each side, and deciding to just pass explicit coordinates with the head bone assignment rather than fuss with directional keywords.

Now I'm mapping out the neck and head positions in world space, defining a path from the chest up through the neck joints to the head point, adjusting the head's facing direction to look slightly raised and alert.

I'm checking the overall proportions against a real wolf's dimensions and realizing my build is too chunky and tall compared to actual shoulder and head heights, so I'm weighing whether to rescale everything down by a uniform factor to make it more realistic.

Redoing the body coordinates with smaller, more grounded numbers—shifting hips, withers, and spine path lower so the shoulder height lands closer to a realistic 0.85-0.88 range instead of the overtall version I had.

Settling on 0.9 at withers as a believable large wolf scale, I'm now laying out the actual spine, chest, and neck coordinates to build the body curve from hips through shoulders toward the head base.

Continuing to head placement: skull center sits forward and up with top around 1.15 and ears reaching 1.28, giving a nicely alert posture relative to the shoulder height. Now I'm starting on the neck ruff, planning fur card geometry wrapped around the neck for texture.

For the fur tuft shape, I'm designing a tapered spiky lock as an SVG path in a tall thin viewbox, keeping the drawing in grayscale so it can be tinted by the coat color read from the root paint, using a vertical gradient from darker gray at the base to near-white at the tip for a soft multiplied-tint look.

Now I'm sketching out card placements: scattering card clusters across the neck sweep with filters for direction and spacing, then planning similar scatters for a chest ruff, cheek ruff, and a dark dorsal mane line along the spine, each using the coat color and varied lean/bend/flow parameters for natural variation.

Then I'm scattering cards on the body surface with a lighter, smaller profile for back-lying fur, plus tail cards, and designing the tail chain shape with a bushy radius taper and a color gradient that shifts to a darker tip near the end.

I want to add a dorsal stripe using angular sectors over a limited range of the tail, layering that against the bands for the tip color, while checking whether the sector coloring would override the tip shading where their ranges overlap.

For the tail, I'm mapping out chain path points for three spans tapering toward the tip, tagged as tail1/tail2/tail3, confirming the tail starts at the hips without clashing with the body's end point.

For the eyes, I'm thinking of giving the wolf amber, slightly glowing eyes with a dark pupil, likely using a small amber sphere with subtle emissive glow rather than a decal for simplicity.

I'm now working out the eye placement geometrically, computing where the skull's ellipsoid surface intersects near the eye socket coordinates so the eyeball sits embedded correctly, and considering using a surface query helper to find the exact hit point on the skull mesh for placement.

Then I'm layering the pupil as a smaller black sphere positioned slightly outward from the eyeball's surface normal, embedding it partially so it protrudes just enough above the eye's own surface.

For the eyebrows I'm placing a dark rod/wedge shape above each eye, computing inner and outer endpoints relative to the eye position and mirroring across the side with the s*sign, slanting it slightly to read as alert rather than angry.

For eye depth I'm layering a dark flattened sphere as a socket rim embedded behind the eyeball, with the amber iris sphere sitting on top so the eye reads with proper socket shading and slight protrusion.

Now I'm setting up a small scaled sphere at the muzzle tip for the nose, flattened slightly to fit the snout shape.

I'm also working out the muzzle's geometry against the skull - placing the skull center and figuring the muzzle's length and radius tapering toward the tip, checking whether the total head length from back of skull to nose tip is proportional.

Now I'm positioning the nose and defining the lower jaw path, sweeping from the jaw joint toward the muzzle tip with tapering radii, matching the jaw bottom to the muzzle's underside.

Writing face paint logic...

Picking a cool blue-grey palette for the fur with darker bridge accents and cream undertones for a stylized wolf look.

Rather than accessories that might make it look domesticated, I'll give it rugged hand-painted details instead: a scar across the muzzle, a notched left ear, visible claws, and spiky fur tufts to sell the wild, weathered character.

Still refining ear geometry...

Checking the orthogonality works out, with the cross product giving a thickness direction mostly along +Z as needed. For the inner ear, I'll use the same orientation but a smaller offset outline pushed slightly forward with less thickness.

Now I'm coloring the inner ear a pink-cream tone and defining a smaller nested outline shape for it, reusing it for both ears and skipping extra details like fur tufts or whiskers. Moving on to paws, I'm placing a base ellipsoid at each foot position and planning four small toe spheres per paw.

Each paw gets toes positioned in an arc with dark claw spikes pointing forward-down, bringing the part count to about nine pieces per paw times four paws—well within budget—so I'm thinking about writing a helper to merge the toe geometry together per paw to keep things efficient.

I'll skip actual mesh merging for now since part count is fine, and attach each foot to the leg's tip joint, falling back to the last joint if tip isn't defined. For hind legs, I need to set the foot target height so the paw ellipsoid center sits correctly relative to the ankle joint, and I'm deciding to skip dewclaws and carpal pads for simplicity.

I'm scattering small leaning fur-tuft cards along the hind leg hock and front leg elbow/forearm sweeps, filtering by surface normal and height to create a feathered look, then setting up the sweep object for leg geometry with its paint color. For the body, I'm adding a cream chest bib by blending coat paint based on a smoothstep gradient for the chest front lightening.

I'm also adding a dark dorsal saddle band using noise-perturbed normal thresholds to give the edges an irregular, hand-painted feel, blended against the gray base with flank areas kept lighter. I'm considering adding subtle lighting-style shading—lightening near the top where normals point up and darkening under the belly—but since the belly is meant to stay cream, I'll skip the shadow blend there to avoid muddying the color.

Now I'm layering in a rim highlight for steep upward-facing normals, then thinking through how to paint fine fur striations: using a grain texture oriented along the body's z-axis to create directional streaks, resolving that nested paint into a plain color before mixing it with the darker saddle tone. I'm estimating texel density based on the wolf's surface area to pick a grain size fine enough (~1.5mm texels) to read as realistic fur grain without being too costly.

I'm also sketching out ruff tuft card textures as simple SVGs—gradient-tinted tapered shapes representing individual fur locks—kept in greyscale so they can be tinted per-part, while watching the total flat color count and card hit count stay within budget for the neck area.

Now I'm estimating triangle counts from bent cards across neck, chest, and body regions, confirming the mesh stays lightweight even at hundreds of cards, and planning the mouth interior as a short dark rod placed inside the parted jaw to suggest depth without full tongue/whisker geometry.

For teeth, I'm sketching small canine spikes positioned at the muzzle and jaw bones with opposing directions to fit the slight jaw opening, and considering whether tiny spheres could stand in for an incisor row.

I'm also thinking about adding boots and blaze markings on the chest, deciding to skip the dorsal crest cards and belly tuck shift since they're not worth the complexity, and starting to work out the body radius profile along its length.

Writing spine interpolation math...

Tapering the neck radii so it narrows smoothly into the chest without overlapping, and planning denser mane cards plus making sure the skull geometry fully covers the neck joint.

I'm figuring out the spine chain naming—hips as the root with no special role, then spine1 through spine3 up to chest as the tip joint—and building the chain with a catmull path through those points. For legs, I'm deciding the front legs should parent off the spine's chest tip, using the shoulder and chest z-positions to line up the joint hierarchy correctly.

For the limbs, I'm deciding front legs attach to the chest and hind legs attach to the hips, with bend directions for each joint (elbow back, wrist forward, knee forward, hock back) so the IK solves naturally in the sagittal plane. I'm also working out the joint name arrays for each limb—shoulder, elbow, wrist, paw for front legs and hip, knee, hock, foot for hind legs—parameterized by side.

Now I'm sketching the paw geometry function, placing small sphere joints and toe offsets relative to the foot position.

Checking the paw ellipsoid and toe sphere dimensions to make sure their bottoms align just above the ground, verifying the math on radii and scale factors so the claws sit correctly at the tips.

I'm settling on paw colors with a darker gray-brown tone, placing hind paw positions relative to hip offset, and narrowing front leg spacing to fit inside the body width. I'm also planning to add spiky dark hackle cards along the back for extra fur detail.

For facial markings, I'm skipping an asymmetric scar idea and instead adding small pale eyebrow spots above each eye, a classic wolf-like marking, computed by checking distance from fixed brow points near the eyes.

I'm also setting up ear coloring so the outer ear is mostly gray but darkens toward the tip based on local surface height, then moving on to neck ruff scatter placement and figuring out where to scatter small decorative elements on the skull surface using filters based on position and surface normal to keep them off the front face and lower jaw.

Scattering card elements for the chest ruff, back fur, and tail tuft, tuning counts, minimum distances, sizes, lean angles, and flow directions for each region so the fur reads as pointing down on the chest and outward along the back and tail.

For the tail color, I'm defining a custom paint function that blends the normal coat color into a dark tip shade near the tail's end using a smoothstep gradient based on z-position, rather than using discrete color bands.

For the rig, I'm making sure bone names stay unique, adding a slight jaw rotation pose at the end, and setting up the eye glow effect on the stick part with a modest intensity. The head joint parents off the neck's second joint, using that joint's chain point as the attachment position, with distinct head and jaw roles defined.

I'm aligning the neck chain's starting point to match the spine's endpoint exactly, verifying the neck angles upward and forward as expected, and double-checking that paw contact points sit at ground level while the tail tip rests comfortably above it. I still need to work out the skull part before computing eye placement, and I should watch for strict TypeScript unused variable errors as I go.

Now I'm trimming imports down to only what's actually used—keeping catmull for the spine path and rng, but dropping unused helpers like frame or offset. Writing the fur and coat paint functions...

Still writing shading code...

Still writing leg shading logic...

I'm getting the skull's surface point for eye placement using a forward-lateral azimuth and elevation, then attaching a small sphere to represent the eye at that hit point, embedded partway into the bone.

Now I'm layering a smaller amber sphere for the iris with a glow effect, then positioning the black pupil slightly offset along the eye's facing normal, calculating protrusion based on the sphere's embed depth.

Since the sinking logic is ambiguous for spheres, I decide to sidestep it entirely and position the eyes explicitly using an offset helper that pushes the sphere out along the hit normal, avoiding the sink/embed math altogether.

Now I'm layering the pupil, rim, and highlight at slightly different outward offsets so each protrudes just enough to read as a convincing eye without clipping into the surface beneath it.

For the brow ridge, I'm switching from the stick helper to an explicit capsule part so I can override the cap style to round instead of flat.

I'm computing brow endpoints offset from the eye hit point rather than the raw eye center, slanting the inner point lower and the outer point higher to give the brow a natural outward lift, even if it risks minor floating or overlap with the skull surface.

Now I'm placing the eyes using the skull ellipsoid's center and radii, checking that the azimuth/elevation puts them close to where the muzzle begins, which works fine for a wolf-like profile. Then I'm positioning the ear base near the top-back of the skull.

For the muzzle, I'm sweeping a tapered shape from the face down to the nose area using two control points with shrinking radii, applying the face color and rounded caps, bound to the head bone. Finally I'm adding a small flattened sphere for the nose, darkened and scaled to sit at the muzzle tip.

I'll skip tiny nostril details, nose highlights, chin tufts, and whiskers to keep complexity manageable, estimating around 120 parts total. I'll still add a few extra touches like hock tufts and neck scruff for visual richness, but hold off on dewclaws unless there's time.

For facial detail, I'm considering a dark lip line along the muzzle but ultimately skipping it, and attempting to paint battle scars onto the flank coat as diagonal slash marks using positional math on the left side.

Simplifying the scar logic...

Now I'm working out the rig composition, checking that the limb and chain functions accept point arrays properly, then sketching a leg builder function that takes a root point, foot position, segment lengths, and bend parameters.

Adding haunch and shoulder spheres for the body shape...

Now I'm defining the tail chain segments with tapering radii and a rounded tip, then setting up scattered fluff cards along the neck sweep for a ruff effect. I'll finish with SVG textures and the final metadata block—name "Gray Wolf (Alert)", description, and style—before writing the file.

I'm sketching out the ear construction function, extruding an outline shape with bevel and thickness onto the head bone, using typed outline point tuples with sharp corner markers, plus a notched variant. Writing paint functions and color mixing for the ears and tail coat...

Now I'm building the eye geometry: looping over both left and right sides, finding the skull hit point, then layering spheres outward for the eye rim, an amber glow, a black pupil, and a highlight offset slightly from the surface normal.

After the eyes, I'll move to writing the file and scattering surface details across the rest of the body once all parts exist, filtering chest card placements by position and normal direction.
